claim: Intravital microscopy can provide unique insights into the function of biological processes in a native context.
source: Intravital microscopy can provide unique insights into the function of biological processes in a native context.
evidence: This is a general statement about the capabilities of intravital microscopy, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Physiological motion caused by peristalsis, respiration and the heartbeat can present a significant challenge for functional readouts such as fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM).
source: However, physiological motion caused by peristalsis, respiration and the heartbeat can present a significant challenge, particularly for functional readouts such as fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM), which require longer acquisition times to obtain a quantitative readout.
evidence: This statement describes a known challenge in the field based on the technical requirements of FLIM.

claim: FLIM requires longer acquisition times to obtain a quantitative readout.
source: However, physiological motion caused by peristalsis, respiration and the heartbeat can present a significant challenge, particularly for functional readouts such as fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM), which require longer acquisition times to obtain a quantitative readout.
evidence: This is a technical characteristic of FLIM imaging that is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Galene is a versatile multi-platform software tool for image-based correction of sample motion blurring in time resolved and conventional laser scanning fluorescence microscopy data in two and three dimensions.
source: Here, we present and benchmark Galene, a versatile multi-platform software tool for image-based correction of sample motion blurring in both time resolved and conventional laser scanning fluorescence microscopy data in two and three dimensions.
evidence: This is the main claim about the software tool developed in this work, supported by the data and demonstrations presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Galene is able to resolve intravital FLIM-FRET images of intra-abdominal organs in murine models subject to physiological motions.
source: We show that Galene is able to resolve intravital FLIM-FRET images of intra-abdominal organs in murine models and NADH autofluorescence of human dermal tissue imaging subject to a wide range of physiological motions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures throughout the manuscript demonstrating correction of FLIM-FRET images in murine organs.

claim: Galene is able to resolve NADH autofluorescence of human dermal tissue imaging subject to a wide range of physiological motions.
source: We show that Galene is able to resolve intravital FLIM-FRET images of intra-abdominal organs in murine models and NADH autofluorescence of human dermal tissue imaging subject to a wide range of physiological motions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 demonstrating correction of human skin autofluorescence imaging.

claim: Galene can enable FLIM imaging in situations where a stable imaging platform is not always possible.
source: Thus, Galene can enable FLIM imaging in situations where a stable imaging platform is not always possible and rescue previously discarded quantitative imaging data.
evidence: This is inferred from the demonstrated ability of Galene to correct for motion in various challenging imaging scenarios presented in the manuscript.

claim: Galene can rescue previously discarded quantitative imaging data.
source: Thus, Galene can enable FLIM imaging in situations where a stable imaging platform is not always possible and rescue previously discarded quantitative imaging data.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the capability of the software to correct motion artifacts that would have previously rendered data unusable.

claim: Genetically-expressed FRET-based biosensors enable researchers to probe signalling events in native tissues.
source: Genetically-expressed Förster resonant energy transfer (FRET)-based biosensors enable researchers to probe signalling events in native tissues (Conway et al., 2017; Ellenbroek and van Rheenen, 2014; Nobis et al., 2018) where they can provide spatio-temporal information about drug target response in a tumour (Conway et al., 2018, 2014; Hirata et al., 2015; Nobis et al., 2017, 2013) or dynamic signalling events in migrating cells (Mizuno et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work in the field.

claim: FRET-based biosensors can provide spatio-temporal information about drug target response in a tumour.
source: Genetically-expressed Förster resonant energy transfer (FRET)-based biosensors enable researchers to probe signalling events in native tissues (Conway et al., 2017; Ellenbroek and van Rheenen, 2014; Nobis et al., 2018) where they can provide spatio-temporal information about drug target response in a tumour (Conway et al., 2018, 2014; Hirata et al., 2015; Nobis et al., 2017, 2013) or dynamic signalling events in migrating cells (Mizuno et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work demonstrating this application.

claim: FRET-based biosensors can provide information about dynamic signalling events in migrating cells.
source: Genetically-expressed Förster resonant energy transfer (FRET)-based biosensors enable researchers to probe signalling events in native tissues (Conway et al., 2017; Ellenbroek and van Rheenen, 2014; Nobis et al., 2018) where they can provide spatio-temporal information about drug target response in a tumour (Conway et al., 2018, 2014; Hirata et al., 2015; Nobis et al., 2017, 2013) or dynamic signalling events in migrating cells (Mizuno et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Mizuno et al., 2016).

claim: Time resolved imaging of NADH autofluorescence can be used to probe the metabolic state of cells.
source: Time resolved imaging of NADH autofluorescence (Blacker and Duchen, 2016; Skala et al., 2007) can be used to probe the metabolic state of cells and multispectral imaging (Patalay et al., 2012) has been investigated for the diagnosis of dermatitis and malignant melanoma (König, 2012), among other applications.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Blacker and Duchen, 2016; Skala et al., 2007).

claim: Multispectral imaging has been investigated for the diagnosis of dermatitis and malignant melanoma.
source: Time resolved imaging of NADH autofluorescence (Blacker and Duchen, 2016; Skala et al., 2007) can be used to probe the metabolic state of cells and multispectral imaging (Patalay et al., 2012) has been investigated for the diagnosis of dermatitis and malignant melanoma (König, 2012), among other applications.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Patalay et al., 2012; König, 2012).

claim: Hyperspectral imaging can be used to extract microenvironmental information from autofluorescence.
source: Hyperspectral imaging, time resolved imaging in multiple spectral channels, can be used to extract microenvironmental information from autofluorescence (Cutrale et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Cutrale et al., 2017).

claim: FLIM techniques depend on measuring small changes in the fluorescence signal, often necessitating relatively long integration times.
source: These techniques depend on measuring small changes in the fluorescence signal, such as a small change in lifetime or change in spectral properties. Consequently, more signal is required to determine the parameters of interest, often necessitating relatively long integration times.
evidence: This is a technical characteristic of FLIM that is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Long integration times required for FLIM have proved to be a significant constraint to the uptake of FLIM in intravital microscopy.
source: This requirement has proved to be a significant constraint to the uptake of FLIM in intravital microscopy, where physiological motion due to, for example peristalsis, respiration or the heartbeat can induce significant motion during the image acquisition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical challenges described and the known limitations in the field.

claim: Physiological motion can often be tolerated in intensity-based imaging where acquisition times are short.
source: This motion can often be tolerated in intensity-based imaging where acquisition times are short.
evidence: This is a comparison based on established knowledge about different imaging modalities.

claim: When an image must be integrated over tens or hundreds of seconds, sample motion rapidly renders the image unintelligible.
source: However, when an image must be integrated over tens or even hundreds of seconds, sample motion rapidly renders the image unintelligible.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the physics of image acquisition and is demonstrated in the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Physical restraints such as tissue clamping or the application of negative pressure may be used to limit sample motion.
source: While physical restraints such as tissue clamping or the application of negative pressure, may be used to limit the sample motion to a degree, this approach is not always effective to the extent required for high resolution microscopy and, in some cases, can compromise the sample integrity.
evidence: This describes existing approaches in the field, representing established knowledge and practice.

claim: Physical restraints to limit sample motion are not always effective to the extent required for high resolution microscopy.
source: While physical restraints such as tissue clamping or the application of negative pressure, may be used to limit the sample motion to a degree, this approach is not always effective to the extent required for high resolution microscopy and, in some cases, can compromise the sample integrity.
evidence: This is based on practical experience and knowledge in the field about the limitations of physical restraint methods.

claim: Physical restraints to limit sample motion can in some cases compromise the sample integrity.
source: While physical restraints such as tissue clamping or the application of negative pressure, may be used to limit the sample motion to a degree, this approach is not always effective to the extent required for high resolution microscopy and, in some cases, can compromise the sample integrity.
evidence: This is based on practical experience and knowledge in the field about potential negative effects of physical restraint methods.

claim: The motion correction approach using Galene can be applied directly to data acquired on existing commercial and clinical FLIM and conventional fluorescence microscopy systems in two and three dimensions in post processing.
source: Here, we describe a motion blurring compensation approach using image-based realignment that can be applied directly to data acquired on existing commercial and clinical FLIM and conventional fluorescence microscopy systems in two and three dimensions in post processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by the demonstrations throughout the manuscript using data from multiple commercial systems.

claim: FLIM is most commonly implemented using laser scanning microscopy (LSM).
source: FLIM is most commonly implemented using laser scanning microscopy (LSM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the typical implementation of FLIM.

claim: To acquire sufficient number of photons in FLIM, an image is constructed by integrating the photon signal over many frames.
source: To acquire sufficient number of photons, an image is constructed by integrating the photon signal over many frames (passes over the scan area).
evidence: This describes the technical approach used in FLIM imaging, representing established knowledge.

claim: A typical FLIM image may take several minutes to acquire.
source: A typical FLIM image may take several minutes to acquire and so is susceptible to motion blurring from physiological motion.
evidence: This is a practical observation about typical FLIM acquisition times based on field knowledge.

claim: Rigid body image registration has been applied to correct for slow motion relative to the frame rate in LSM time series acquisitions.
source: (i) Where the motion is slow relative to the frame rate, (e.g. a slow drift), rigid body image registration (Thévenaz et al., 1998) or feature-based registration such as Scale Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT)-based algorithms have been applied to correct for the motion,
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Thévenaz et al., 1998).

claim: When motion is intermittent, frames captured during the motion may be automatically detected and excluded from the time series.
source: (ii) When the motion is intermittent, frames captured during the motion may be automatically detected and excluded from the time series (Soulet et al., 2013),
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Soulet et al., 2013).

claim: When motion is fast relative to the frame rate, each frame will appear distorted as the sample moves while the laser is scanned across the field of view.
source: (iii) When the motion is fast relative to the frame rate, each frame will appear distorted as the sample moves while the laser is scanned across the field of view.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the physics of laser scanning microscopy.

claim: Advanced approaches using Hidden-Markov-Models, Lucas–Kanade framework, or algorithms based on Lie groups have been employed to correct for fast motion in LSM.
source: In this case, more advanced approaches that model the intra-frame motion using methods such as Hidden-Markov-Models (Dombeck et al., 2007), the Lucas–Kanade framework (Greenberg and Kerr, 2009), or algorithms based on Lie groups (Vercauteren et al., 2006) have been employed.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Dombeck et al., 2007; Greenberg and Kerr, 2009; Vercauteren et al., 2006).

claim: Previous motion correction techniques have not been applied to FLIM data.
source: These techniques have not, to date, been applied to FLIM data.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: During conventional FLIM acquisition, histograms of photon arrival times are typically accumulated to produce a single image, and blurring due to sample motion is 'baked into' the data and cannot be compensated.
source: This is because during FLIM acquisition, histograms of photon arrival times are typically accumulated to produce a single image. In this approach, blurring due to sample motion is 'baked into' the data and thus cannot be compensated.
evidence: This describes a technical limitation of conventional FLIM acquisition approaches.

claim: Improved device-computer bandwidth and storage have enabled the recording of individual photon arrival times and markers associated with the scan frame and line clocks.
source: More recently, however, improved device-computer bandwidth and storage have enabled the recording of individual photon arrival times and markers associated with the scan frame and line clocks (Becker et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Becker et al., 2006).

claim: Most modern commercial time-correlated single photon counting (TCSPC) FLIM systems support time-tagged mode, often by default.
source: Most modern commercial time-correlated single photon counting (TCSPC) FLIM systems support this mode, often by default.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of commercial FLIM systems based on field knowledge.

claim: Galene reconstructs each frame from time-tagged FLIM data and determines the motion both between and within each frame using an approach based on the Lucas-Kanade framework.
source: Here, we describe an approach whereby we reconstruct each frame from this time-tagged FLIM data and determine the motion both between and within each frame using an approach based on the Lucas-Kanade framework (Baker and Matthews, 2004).
evidence: This describes the technical approach used in Galene, with citation to the Lucas-Kanade framework.

claim: Galene can be used to correct for motion in two- and three-dimensional FLIM data collected using widely deployed commercial systems.
source: We have implemented these algorithms in a new open source package, Galene, which can be used to correct for motion in two- and three-dimensional FLIM data collected using widely deployed commercial systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by demonstrations throughout the manuscript using data from multiple commercial systems.

claim: Galene may be used to correct conventional fluorescence microscopy data using intravital 3D multispectral imaging data.
source: While the main focus of this manuscript is motion correction of time resolved data, we show that Galene may also be used to correct conventional fluorescence microscopy data using intravital 3D multispectral imaging data of labelled immune cells in the murine lymph node highlighting its wider application for intravital imaging applications.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 demonstrating correction of multispectral imaging data.

claim: FLIM data are acquired in a time-tagged time-resolved (TTTR) mode whereby each photon arrival time is recorded alongside frame and line markers.
source: We acquire FLIM data in a time-tagged time-resolved (TTTR) mode whereby each photon arrival time is recorded alongside frame and line markers, which allow us to locate each photon within the image.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition method used in this work.

claim: The intensity of each constituent frame is reconstructed from time-tagged data to determine sample motion during image acquisition.
source: From these data, we first reconstruct the intensity of each constituent frame, or, in the 3D case, stack of frames (Figure 1A–C), that make up the image. We use these intensity data to determine the sample motion during the image acquisition relative to a reference stack (Figure 1D–H).
evidence: This describes the method used in Galene and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: A fast, rigid realignment using a 3D generalisation of the phase correlation method is performed first to correct for coarse sample displacements.
source: For each stack, we first perform a fast, rigid realignment using a 3D generalisation of the phase correlation method (Foroosh et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes a step in the Galene algorithm with citation to the phase correlation method.

claim: Rigid realignment cannot correct for sample motion during the stack, which leads to distortions rather than simply displacement of the stack.
source: This corrects for coarse sample displacements but cannot correct for sample motion during the stack, which leads to distortions, rather than simply displacement of the stack.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the nature of rigid transformations and the physics of laser scanning.

claim: Galene uses a fitting approach that accounts explicitly for the raster scan pattern used to acquire the data following the approach of Greenberg and Kerr (2009).
source: To estimate the displacement of the sample during the stack acquisition, we use a fitting approach where we account explicitly for the raster scan pattern used to acquire the data following the approach of Greenberg and Kerr (2009).
evidence: This describes the technical approach used in Galene with citation to prior work.

claim: Galene assumes that the sample moves linearly between a series of initially unknown two- or three-dimensional displacements spaced equally through the scan duration.
source: We assume that the sample moves linearly between a series of initially unknown two- or three-dimensional displacements spaced equally through the scan duration.
evidence: This describes an assumption in the Galene algorithm.

claim: Galene uses a trust-region non-linear optimisation algorithm to determine the sample motion during stack acquisition.
source: We can then determine the sample motion during the stack acquisition by finding the set of displacements which minimises the difference between the corrected stack and the reference stack using a trust-region non-linear optimisation algorithm.
evidence: This describes the optimization method used in Galene.

claim: Galene uses a variant of the inverse-compositional Lucas-Kanade algorithm to perform optimisation efficiently.
source: To perform this optimisation efficiently we use a variant of the inverse-compositional Lucas-Kanade algorithm (Lucas and Kanade, 1981), used extensively in image registration applications (Baker and Matthews, 2004);
evidence: This describes the algorithm used in Galene with citations to prior work.

claim: The inverse-compositional Lucas-Kanade algorithm uses the gradient of the reference stack rather than calculating the gradient of the interpolated stack at every iteration, which is computationally expensive.
source: its key insight is that, rather than calculating the gradient of the interpolated stack at every iteration, a computationally expensive procedure, we can instead use the gradient of the reference stack, which is of course invariant (Baker and Matthews, 2004).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the algorithm with citation to prior work.

claim: The effective dwell time in each pixel varies across the image due to sample motion.
source: We use the displacement information to determine the effective dwell time in each pixel (which will vary across the image due to the sample motion).
evidence: This is a logical consequence of sample motion during acquisition.

claim: Monte Carlo simulations were used to determine the range of amplitudes and frequencies of sample motion that can be reliably corrected by Galene.
source: To determine the range of amplitudes and frequencies of sample motion that can be reliably corrected, we used Monte Carlo simulations of FLIM data in the presence of sample motion (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the simulation approach used to evaluate Galene's performance.

claim: The heartrate of an adult mouse anaesthetized under ~1% isoflurane is approximately 350 bpm (~6 Hz).
source: We compare these results with reference to average values for physiological events known to impair image acquisition; the heartrate (red arrow, 350 bpm, ~6 Hz) and respiratory rate (blue arrow, 60 bpm, 1 Hz) of an adult mouse anaesthetized under ~1% isoflurane (Ewald et al., 2011) are shown.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Ewald et al., 2011).

claim: The respiratory rate of an adult mouse anaesthetized under ~1% isoflurane is approximately 60 bpm (1 Hz).
source: We compare these results with reference to average values for physiological events known to impair image acquisition; the heartrate (red arrow, 350 bpm, ~6 Hz) and respiratory rate (blue arrow, 60 bpm, 1 Hz) of an adult mouse anaesthetized under ~1% isoflurane (Ewald et al., 2011) are shown.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Ewald et al., 2011).

claim: Galene can compensate for motion parallel to the fast axis more effectively than motion parallel to the slow axis.
source: We observed that the system could compensate for motion parallel to the fast axis (0°) more effectively than motion parallel to the slow axis (90°);
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Motion in the slow axis results in whole lines of the sample being sampled either twice or not at all.
source: this is unsurprising as motion in the slow axis will result in whole lines of the sample being sampled either twice or not at all.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the raster scan pattern used in laser scanning microscopy.

claim: The range of amplitudes and frequencies that Galene is able to correct covers a broad range of physiologically relevant motions commonly observed during functional intravital imaging.
source: We note that the range of amplitudes and frequencies that Galene is able to correct covers a broad range of physiologically relevant motions commonly observed during functional intravital imaging and will therefore be of use in a range of in vivo imaging applications.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results shown in Figure 2 compared to physiological motion parameters.

claim: Galene can correct for a significantly larger range of motions than StackReg, SIFT, and SIMA packages.
source: However, Galene is able to correct for significantly larger sample motions than SIMA (compare Figure 2—figure supplement 1Aiv, SIMA and v, Galene), for example the larger motion shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, corresponding to a larger motion induced by the heartbeat, and so will be useful in a broader range of intravital experimental conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: StackReg and SIFT are only able to correct for low frequency motion as they correct for rigid transformations between frames.
source: StackReg and SIFT both correct for rigid transformations between each frame and so are unable to cope with the distortion produced by LSM with a moving sample; consequently, these packages are only able to correct for low frequency motion (as, for example, encountered during slow sample drifts where the observed motion artefact can be approximated by a linear transformation (for example, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: SIMA uses a HMM model which uses information about the laser scan pattern and is able to cope with a larger range of motion than StackReg and SIFT.
source: SIMA uses a HMM model which uses information about the laser scan pattern and so is able to cope with a larger range of motion (for example, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, equivalent to a small displacement caused by the heartbeat).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Titanium windows enable longitudinal imaging of abdominal organs.
source: We acquired images through surgically implanted titanium windows (see schematic in Figure 3) that enable longitudinal imaging of abdominal organs (Ritsma et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Ritsma et al., 2014).

claim: Imaging abdominal organs through an optical window is challenging as they experience considerable motion as a result of physiological activity in nearby organs such as respiration and the heartbeat.
source: Imaging abdominal organs through an optical window is challenging as they experience considerable motion as a result of physiological activity in nearby organs such as respiration and the heartbeat.
evidence: This is based on practical experience and knowledge in the field.

claim: Finding areas sufficiently stable to acquire FLIM images through optical windows significantly limits the usable area of the window.
source: Simply finding areas sufficiently stable to acquire FLIM images significantly limits the usable area of the window, and, in some cases, can render mice completely unusable.
evidence: This is based on practical experience described in the manuscript.

claim: Motion dominated by the heartbeat has a frequency of 5.4 Hz and peak-peak amplitude of 27 μm (approximately 10% of the FOV) in pancreatic tissue imaging.
source: We performed an amplitude-spectrum analysis on the estimated displacements (Figure 3B,C) and found motion of (i) a frequency of 5.4 Hz and peak-peak amplitude of 27 μm (approximately 10% of the FOV), corresponding to the heartbeat
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Motion dominated by respiration and peristalsis has frequencies from 0.2 to 2.2 Hz with an average peak-peak amplitude of 42 μm (approximately 15% of the field of view) in pancreatic tissue imaging.
source: and (ii) slower motions with a range of frequencies from 0.2 to 2.2 Hz with an average peak-peak amplitude of 42 μm (approximately 15% of the field of view), corresponding to respiration.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: For faster but smaller motion due to the heartbeat, Galene can correct for motion equally well at all scan rates tested (700, 1000, and 1400 Hz).
source: We found that for the faster but smaller motion due to the heartbeat we were able to correct for motion equally well at all scan rates (see Figure 3D, average correlation quantified in Figure 3Div).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: For larger motion due to respiration and peristalsis, successful correction was only obtained at 1400 Hz scan rates, with partial correction at 1000 Hz and effectively no correction at 700 Hz.
source: For the larger due to respiration and peristalsis, we found that we were only able to successfully correct for motion at 1400 Hz scan rates; partial correction was obtained at 1000 Hz and effectively no correction at 700 Hz (see Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: For larger motions it may be helpful to acquire at a faster frame rate where possible.
source: Underscoring the simulated data results, these data indicate that for larger motions it may be helpful to acquire at a faster frame rate where possible.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing better correction at higher scan rates for larger motions.

claim: At 700 Hz, realignment is significantly improved when motion is aligned with the fast axis compared to the slow axis.
source: At 700 Hz the realignment is significantly improved when the motion is aligned with the fast axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: At 1400 Hz, motion is corrected equally well whether aligned with the fast or slow axis.
source: At 1400 Hz, when the motion is slower relative to the scan rate, the motion is corrected equally well in either case.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: It is important to use a fast scan rate where possible for motion correction.
source: This highlights both the importance of using a fast scan rate where possible and, where there is a clear direction of motion, approximately aligning it with the scanner fast axis by rotating the scanner field of view.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing the effect of scan rate on correction quality.

claim: Where there is a clear direction of motion, approximately aligning it with the scanner fast axis by rotating the scanner field of view can improve correction.
source: This highlights both the importance of using a fast scan rate where possible and, where there is a clear direction of motion, approximately aligning it with the scanner fast axis by rotating the scanner field of view.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing the effect of motion direction on correction quality.

claim: There was a slight improvement in the average correlation with increasing number of realignment points up to 20 points for 256 × 256 images.
source: For images of this size, there was a slight improvement in the average correlation with increasing number of realignment points up to 20 points.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Using 40 realignment points, the correlation was slightly reduced compared to 20 points for 256 × 256 images.
source: Using 40 points, however, the correlation was slightly reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Using a very large number of realignment points can be detrimental as there is not enough information to accurately determine the motion at each point.
source: Using a very large number of realignment points can be detrimental; as the number of points increases, the number of pixels which constrain each point is reduced and eventually there is not enough information to accurately determine the motion at each point.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the nature of the optimization problem.

claim: Using between 5–20 realignment points for 256 × 256 images and 10–20 points for 512 × 512 images was sufficient to obtain good correction over a broad range of conditions.
source: In general, we found that using between 5–20 realignment points for 256 × 256 images and 10–20 points for 512 × 512 images was sufficient to obtain good correction over a broad range of conditions.
evidence: This is based on empirical testing described in the manuscript.

claim: A Gaussian smoothing kernel may optionally be applied to each frame before realignment to improve the realignment when signal to noise level is low.
source: As the signal to noise level in each frame of a FLIM image is often low due to the restricted count rate requirements of TCSPC imaging, a Gaussian smoothing kernel may optionally be applied to each frame before realignment to improve the realignment.
evidence: This describes an optional feature of the Galene algorithm.

claim: A noticeable improvement in the realignment result was found using a smoothing kernel of width 2 or 4 pixels compared to no smoothing.
source: We found a noticeable improvement in the realignment result using a kernel of with 2 or 4 pixels compared to no smoothing.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Using excessively large smoothing kernels can reduce the quality of the realignment as the contrast in the image is reduced.
source: At larger kernel sizes, the correlation gradually reduced; using excessively large smoothing kernels can reduce the quality of the realignment as the contrast in the image is reduced.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of excessive smoothing and is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Using a smoothing kernel of 2–4 pixels works well over a broad range of conditions.
source: We have found that using a smoothing kernel of 2–4 pixels works well over a broad range of conditions.
evidence: This is based on empirical testing described in the manuscript.

claim: Rac1 regulates a diverse array of cellular events including the cell cycle, cell-cell adhesion, motility and differentiation.
source: Rac1 regulates a diverse array of cellular events including the cell cycle, cell-cell adhesion, motility and differentiation (Heasman and Ridley, 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Heasman and Ridley, 2008).

claim: Rac1 has been shown to be a key driver of Wnt-induced stem cell activation within the intestinal crypt.
source: and has been shown to be a key driver of Wnt-induced stem cell activation within the intestinal crypt (Myant et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Myant et al., 2013).

claim: The Rac1 biosensor contains an ECFP donor, which has a complex decay profile dominated by contributions from two conformations with similar spectral profiles.
source: The Rac1 biosensor contains an ECFP donor, which has a complex decay profile, dominated by contributions from two conformations with similar spectral profiles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ECFP fluorophore.

claim: The FRET efficiencies of the Rac1 GTP (active) and GDP bound (inactive) states were determined to be E = 0.65 and E = 0.02 respectively using global analysis.
source: Using global analysis, we determined the FRET efficiencies of the Rac1 GTP (active) and GDP bound (inactive) states to be E = 0.65 and E = 0.02.
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis performed in this work.

claim: Imaging of the intestine is complicated by motion induced by peristalsis, wave-like contractions of the digestive tract which propel food through the intestine.
source: Imaging of the intestine is further complicated by motion induced by peristalsis, wave-like contractions of the digestive tract which propel food through the intestine.
evidence: This is established knowledge about intestinal physiology.

claim: The gut can be attached only gently to the window as immobilizing a tract of the intestine can obstruct the bowel.
source: The gut can be attached only gently to the window (Ritsma et al., 2012) as immobilizing a tract of the intestine can obstruct the bowel.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Ritsma et al., 2012) and represents practical knowledge.

claim: Occasional large, transient displacements occur during intestinal crypt imaging where the crypt under observation moves completely out of the field of view.
source: When imaging crypts we noted that, alongside persistent smaller motion, occasional large, transient displacements occur where the crypt under observation moves completely out of the field of view (shown in the displacement estimates, Figure 4Aiii);
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Frames where the crypt moves completely out of the field of view cannot be compensated by motion correction.
source: this, of course, cannot be compensated.
evidence: This is a logical limitation of the motion correction approach.

claim: Frames with correlation coefficient less than a threshold value (0.8) are automatically identified and removed from the reconstructed image.
source: We automatically identify and remove these frames by applying a threshold to the correlation between the reference image and the best estimate of the corrected frame, in this case 0.8 (Figure 4Aiv), discarding frames with lower correlation values.
evidence: This describes a feature of the Galene algorithm demonstrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Peristaltic motion continues even ex vivo when the intestine is maintained appropriately for live cell imaging.
source: Peristaltic motion continues even ex vivo when the intestine is maintained appropriately for live cell imaging.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Scopolamine is a small molecule muscarinic antagonist that inhibits the contraction of the smooth muscle layer surrounding the intestine.
source: To inhibit peristalsis for imaging, researchers often use scopolamine, a small molecule muscarinic antagonist that inhibits the contraction of the smooth muscle layer surrounding the intestine (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Wang et al., 2008).

claim: Treatment with scopolamine effectively inhibited peristalsis in ex vivo intestinal tissue.
source: Treatment with scopolamine effectively inhibited peristalsis;
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Treatment with scopolamine induced a significant activation of Rac1 in intestinal tissue compared to untreated tissue.
source: however, unexpectedly we also observed a significant activation of Rac1 in tissue treated with scopolamine compared to untreated tissue (Figure 4D, quantified in E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: The activation of Rac1 by scopolamine was of a similar magnitude to that of tissue treated with phorbol myristate acetate (PMA).
source: This activation was of a similar magnitude to that of tissue treated with phorbol myristate acetate (PMA) (Johnsson et al., 2014), a potent small molecule activator of Rac1.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and comparison to prior work.

claim: The effect of scopolamine on Rac1 activation was also observed when fixed tissue was stained with a Rac1-GTP specific antibody.
source: This effect was also observed when fixed tissue was stained with a Rac1-GTP specific antibody (Myant et al., 2013) (representative images and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pharmacological approaches to reducing sample motion can interfere with the biological process under observation.
source: This interference with Rac1 signalling highlights the need to ensure pharmacological approaches to reducing sample motion do not affect the process under observation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that scopolamine affects Rac1 signaling.

claim: Image based correction can avoid artefacts introduced by pharmacological approaches to inhibiting sample motion.
source: In contrast, by using image based correction, these artefacts can be avoided when looking, for example, at subtle changes in Rac1 GTPase regulation which is known to drive stem cell activity in intestinal crypts (Myant et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between pharmacological and image-based approaches.

claim: Without motion correction, it is extremely difficult to identify subcellular compartments in a majority of the intestinal crypt data.
source: Without motion correction, it is extremely difficult to identify subcellular compartments in a majority of the intestinal crypt data.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: After correcting for motion, subcellular regions and structures in intestinal crypt data can be robustly identified.
source: After correcting for motion, however, we are able to robustly identify subcellular regions and structures in the data.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: A lower level of Rac1 activation was observed in the basal membrane compared to the apical membrane after application of PMA or scopolamine.
source: We observed a lower level of Rac1 activation the basal membrane compared to the apical membrane after application of PMA or scoloplamine, suggesting a potential negative regulation of Rac1 at the basal membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The differential Rac1 activation between basal and apical membranes may be consistent with the critical role of Rac1 in intestinal crypt patterning and differentiation.
source: This may be consistent with the critical role of Rac1 in intestinal crypt patterning and differentiation (de Santa Barbara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data and prior work cited.

claim: Galene provides a significant improvement in the realignment of both in vivo and ex vivo imaging data compared to StackReg and SIMA.
source: Galene produces a significant improvement in the image quality over SIMA and StackReg. In line with the results of our simulations and in addition to enabling correction of time resolved data, Galene demonstrates a significant improvement in the realignment of both in vivo and ex vivo imaging data.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Transient 'priming' using the pharmaceutical Rho kinase inhibitor Fasudil in a model of pancreatic cancer improved response to chemotherapy and impaired metastasis to the liver in an intrasplenic model.
source: In a recent study, we demonstrated that transient 'priming' using the pharmaceutical Rho kinase inhibitor Fasudil in a model of pancreatic cancer (PC) improved response to chemotherapy and impaired metastasis to the liver in an intrasplenic model (Vennin et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Vennin et al., 2017).

claim: Src kinase has been shown to play a critical role in cell adhesion and proliferation in cancer.
source: Src kinase has been shown to play a critical role in cell adhesion and proliferation in cancer (Brunton and Frame, 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Brunton and Frame, 2008).

claim: Src is potentially an anti-invasive target in pancreatic cancer.
source: and is potentially an anti-invasive target in PC (Evans et al., 2012; Morton et al., 2010b; Nobis et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A reduction in Src kinase activity was previously observed in in vitro models of invasion and in end-point xenograft models of a primary tumour imaged using a skin flap technique.
source: We previously observed a reduction in Src kinase activity in in vitro models of invasion and in end-point xenograft models of a primary tumour imaged using a skin flap technique.
evidence: This refers to prior work by the authors.

claim: The reduction in the number of metastases after priming with Fasudil could be, in part, a consequence of a reduction in early adhesion events caused by disruption of Src activation.
source: We therefore hypothesised that the reduction in the number of metastases after priming with Fasudil could be, in part, a consequence of a reduction in early adhesion events caused by disruption of Src activation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on prior observations.

claim: Without correction for sample motion, the assessment of early transient events using FRET is not possible in vivo.
source: However, without correction for sample motion, the assessment of such early transient events using FRET (illustrated schematically in Figure 5B) is not possible in vivo, limiting our ability to quantify colonisation efficiency at this important stage.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations prior to using motion correction.

claim: The liver shows significant motion when imaged behind an optical window due to its proximity to the lungs and heart and attachment to the diaphragm.
source: The liver shows significant motion when imaged behind an optical window due to its proximity to the lungs and heart and attachment to the diaphragm.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge and practical experience.

claim: Motion in the liver frustrates attempts to acquire data for lifetime and hyperspectral unmixing as integration over even a few frames leads to significant image blurring.
source: This frustrates attempts to acquire data for lifetime and hyperspectral unmixing as integration over even a few frames leads to significant image blurring as illustrated in Figure 5Ei.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5E showing the effect of motion on image quality.

claim: A significant increase in Src activity was observed after 8 hr in cancer cells colonising the liver, which was maintained up to 16 hr before plateauing after 24 hr upon spreading.
source: Here, we saw a significant increase in Src activity (increase in Src biosensor lifetime) after 8 hr, which was maintained up to 16 hr before plateauing after 24 hr upon spreading (see Figure 5E, control situation).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G.

claim: Mice treated with Fasudil exhibited a significantly reduced and delayed Src activity compared to those treated with the vehicle.
source: Mice treated with Fasudil exhibited a significantly reduced and delayed Src activity, in line with a delayed spreading phenotype, compared to those treated with the vehicle (see Figure 5Fi, blue-green shift at 8 hr and Figure 5Fii, blue-green shift at 24 hr, quantified in Figure 5G),
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: Src-dependent spreading and activation during the first attachment events in the liver are impaired by treatment with Fasudil.
source: indicating that Src-dependent spreading and activation during the first attachment events in the liver are indeed impaired by treatment with Fasudil.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed reduction in Src activity after Fasudil treatment.

claim: Fasudil priming has a new role in altering adhesion efficiency in secondary sites.
source: These results demonstrate a new role of Fasudil priming in altering adhesion efficiency in secondary sites (Rath et al., 2017; Vennin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with citations to related work.

claim: There is an urgent need to develop anti-metastatic treatments in pancreatic cancer and other metastatic cancer types.
source: There is an urgent need to develop anti-metastatic treatments in PC and other metastatic cancer types (Steeg, 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Steeg, 2016).

claim: Functional intravital microscopy combined with Galene may help development of new strategies to monitor agents that affect critical events preceding colonisation.
source: and functional intravital microscopy combined with Galene may help development of new strategies to monitor agents that affect this critical event preceding colonisation (Ritsma et al., 2012; Steeg et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: Motion during acquisition can cause blurring of the biosensor fluorescence with background autofluorescence which may have a very different lifetime, artificially changing the apparent lifetime of the biosensor.
source: We note that aside from reducing the image quality, motion during acquisition can have a number of more subtle effects: (1) blurring of the biosensor fluorescence with background autofluorescence which may have a very different lifetime can artificially change the apparent lifetime of the biosensor, giving a misleading result
evidence: This is a logical consequence of motion-induced blurring and is demonstrated in the data.

claim: Motion can significantly distort the apparent shape of the cells.
source: and (2) motion can significantly distort the apparent shape of the cells.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of motion during acquisition and is demonstrated in the data.

claim: A reduction in the apparent lifetime of the biosensor was observed due to blurring with the low autofluorescence lifetime of surrounding liver cells.
source: Both artefacts are observed here; we see a reduction in the apparent lifetime of the biosensor due to blurring with the low autofluorescence lifetime of surrounding liver cells
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data comparing corrected and uncorrected images.

claim: An artefactual elongation and apparent spreading of the cancer cell was observed due to motion.
source: and an artefactual elongation and apparent spreading of the cancer cell (compare Figure 5Di–ii) which may lead to an incorrect assumption about their attachment state (see Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data comparing corrected and uncorrected images.

claim: The blurring of the biosensor lifetime with the background autofluorescence leads to an overall reduction in the lifetime in all treatment conditions when data are not motion corrected.
source: The blurring of the biosensor lifetime with the background autofluorescence leads to an overall reduction in the lifetime in all treatment conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data in Figure 5G and 5H.

claim: The magnitude of the effect of motion on lifetime varies greatly from cell to cell depending on the motion and the environment of each cell, leading to significantly higher variance within each condition.
source: As the magnitude of this effect varies greatly from cell to cell depending on the motion and the environment of each cell, we found a significantly higher degree of variance within each condition.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis comparing corrected and uncorrected data.

claim: Increased variability due to motion abolishes the ability to statistically distinguish treatment conditions in Src activity measurements.
source: This increased variability abolishes our ability to statistically distinguish the conditions, highlighting the importance of motion correction to obtain robust results in this context (compare in Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of statistical significance in Figure 5G and 5H.

claim: The lifetime of NADH and FAD autofluorescence can be used as a readout of metabolic activity.
source: The lifetime of NADH and FAD autofluorescence can be used as a readout of metabolic activity (Blacker and Duchen, 2016; Lakowicz et al., 1992; Skala et al., 2007)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Autofluorescence lifetime has potential applications in the detection of precancerous tissue.
source: with potential applications in the detection of precancerous tissue.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications based on established knowledge.

claim: Autofluorescence signal has been investigated in a clinical context for diagnostic purposes using static, flexible and handheld multiphoton microscopes.
source: This autofluorescence signal has been investigated in a clinical context for diagnostic purposes (König, 2012) using static (Patalay et al., 2012), flexible (König et al., 2008) and handheld multiphoton (Sherlock et al., 2015) microscopes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Unlike optical window experiments, the movement observed imaging human skin in an upright configuration occurs isotropically in three dimensions.
source: Unlike optical window experiments, where the inverted imaging configuration and weight of the mouse largely constrains the sample motion to two dimensions, the movement observed imaging human skin in an upright configuration occurs isotropically in three dimensions and so correction for lateral motion alone is insufficient.
evidence: This is based on practical experience and the physics of the imaging configuration.

claim: Two approaches for handling motion in three dimensions are demonstrated: (1) real-time detection and compensation for axial sample motion when imaging a single plane and (2) 3D motion correction within a z-stack.
source: We therefore demonstrate two approaches for handling motion in three dimensions: (1) real-time detection and compensation for axial sample motion when imaging a single plane and (2) 3D motion correction within a z-stack.
evidence: This describes the approaches demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: A handheld multiphoton microscope system incorporates an active (online) axial motion compensation system that corrects for motion in z-axis in real time using OCT-based correction.
source: We recently demonstrated (Sherlock et al., 2015) a handheld multiphoton microscope system that incorporates an active (online) axial motion compensation system that corrects for motion in z-axis in real time. The optical coherence tomography (OCT)-based correction system tracks sample motion perpendicular to the imaging plane in real time and adjusts the objective position to keep the selected plane in focus.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Sherlock et al., 2015).

claim: The combination of active axial motion compensation and software-based lateral motion compensation with Galene is able to effectively remove the motion artefact observed in human skin imaging.
source: The combination of active axial motion compensation and software-based lateral motion compensation is able to effectively remove the motion artefact observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In a clinical setting, it is often desirable to obtain a 3D map of the autofluorescence lifetime to build up structural and functional information resolved into the strata of the skin.
source: In a clinical setting, it is often desirable to obtain a 3D map of the autofluorescence lifetime to build up structural and functional information resolved into the strata of the skin, for example to quantify drug penetrance and delivery (Roberts et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Roberts et al., 2011).

claim: Capturing time-resolved depth stacks with sufficient photon counts can be a time-consuming process, with a 30–50 μm stack taking 10–15 min to acquire.
source: Capturing time-resolved depth stacks with sufficient photon counts can be a time-consuming process; a 30–50 μm stack may take 10–15 min to acquire.
evidence: This is based on practical experience with the imaging system.

claim: A certain degree of motion during 10-15 minute acquisitions is inevitable in live subjects.
source: A certain degree of motion during this period is inevitable in live subjects
evidence: This is a practical observation based on knowledge of live subject imaging.

claim: Conventional frame-by-frame accumulation can lead to both blurring of individual images in the stack and displacement between images in the stack.
source: and, since conventionally each frame is accumulated consecutively (Figure 6Bi), this can lead to both blurring of individual images in the stack and displacement between images in the stack.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of motion during sequential acquisition.

claim: By accumulating a number of scans over the entire stack, motion in three dimensions during each stack acquisition can be estimated and corrected.
source: To overcome this issue, we accumulated a number of scans over the entire stack (Figure 6Bii). We then apply the same motion estimation approach as used in 2D data, extending the displacement points to 3D. Each stack is aligned to a reference stack. Motion in three dimensions during each stack acquisition can then be estimated and corrected.
evidence: This describes the approach used for 3D motion correction demonstrated in Figure 6C.

claim: GPU computation and algorithmic optimisations were used to reduce the processing time for correction of large 3D volumes.
source: To enable correction of these large volumes, we used GPU computation and several algorithmic optimisations to reduce the processing time (see Methods, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes technical improvements made to enable 3D correction.

claim: Galene is able to track and correct for motion in three dimensions during stack acquisition, obtaining undistorted deep-tissue data free from motion artefacts.
source: We see that we are able to track and correct for motion in three dimensions during the stack acquisition, obtaining undistorted deep-tissue data free from motion artefacts.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The approaches demonstrated may enable the use of autofluorescence imaging of other parts of the body more susceptible to sample motion in three dimensions such as the chest.
source: These approaches may enable the use of autofluorescence imaging of other parts of the body more susceptible to sample motion in three dimensions such as the chest.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: Intravital imaging is a crucial tool in immunology, providing unique spatiotemporal information about the localisation, function and interactions between immune cells in their native environment.
source: Intravital imaging is a crucial tool in immunology, providing unique spatiotemporal information about the localisation, function and interactions between immune cells in their native environment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the importance of intravital imaging in immunology.

claim: The organisation and migration of different classes of immune cells within the lymph nodes has been shown to play a critical role in the adaptive immune response.
source: The organisation and migration of different classes of immune cells within the lymph nodes has been shown to play a critical role in the adaptive immune response (Kastenmüller et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Kastenmüller et al., 2012).

claim: The production of antibodies in response to antigen re-exposure after vaccination depends on the interaction between CD4+ T cells and B cells at specific locations in the lymph node.
source: For example, the production of antibodies in response to antigen re-exposure after vaccination depends on the interaction between CD4+ T cells and B cells at a number of specific locations in the lymph node.
evidence: This is established knowledge about immune cell interactions in lymph nodes.

claim: Tracking of immune cell migration is critical to understanding the adaptive immune response and its dysregulation.
source: Tracking of the migration of these cells is therefore critical to understanding this process and its dysregulation.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the importance of cell interactions in the immune response.

claim: Over a 30 minute imaging period of the lymph node, substantial sample motion is observed including slow drift and faster displacements due to physiological motion, primarily respiration.
source: Over this period, substantial sample motion is observed; there is a slow drift due to slight shifts in the immersion liquid meniscus and faster displacements due to physiological motion, primarily respiration.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Imaris 'spot tracking' function was used to track stationary macrophages and use their trajectory to correct for drift.
source: We used the Imaris 'spot tracking' function to track the stationary macrophages and used their trajectory to correct for drift.
evidence: This describes the comparison method used.

claim: Imaris drift correction provides a reduction in the motion artefact, however the correction is not complete.
source: This provides a reduction in the motion artefact, however the correction is not complete (see Figure 7C inset, Video 5),
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C and Video 5.

claim: There is a gradual loss in the correlation between the nominally static capsule signal over time when using Imaris drift correction.
source: and there is a gradual loss in the correlation between the nominally static capsule signal over time (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: Galene provides a significant improvement in the quality of motion correction compared to Imaris drift correction for lymph node imaging data.
source: We then used Galene to correct for the motion based on the static capsule and macrophages and observed a significant improvement in the quality of the correction (see Figure 7D, Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D and Video 5.

claim: Galene will allow more accurate quantification of in vivo cell movement within organs over long imaging periods even in the presence of physiological motion and sample drift.
source: This will allow more accurate quantification of in vivo cell movement within this organ over long imaging periods even in the presence of physiological motion and sample drift.
evidence: This is inferred from the demonstrated improvement in motion correction quality.

claim: Galene uses a fitting approach that explicitly accounts for the raster scan pattern performed by laser scanning microscopes to determine sample motion both between frames and during each frame.
source: Galene uses a fitting approach that explicitly accounting for the raster scan pattern performed by laser scanning microscopes to determine sample motion both between frames and during each frame.
evidence: This describes the technical approach used in Galene.

claim: Using the motion estimate, both FLIM and intensity-based data can be reconstructed, allowing quantitative analysis free from artefacts introduced by motion.
source: Using the motion estimate, both FLIM and intensity-based data can be reconstructed, allowing quantitative analysis free from artefacts introduced by motion.
evidence: This describes the capability of Galene demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: Two modifications were implemented to scale the approach to motion correction across 3D volumes: GPU acceleration and exploiting the structure of the optimisation problem.
source: To scale this approach to motion correction across 3D volumes where there may be thousands of displacement points, we implement two modifications. First, we take advantage of graphical co-processors to accelerate computationally intensive sections of the motion correction algorithm using to take advantage of graphical co-processors. We then exploit the structure of the optimisation problem to radically reduce the computational burden of estimating each optimisation step.
evidence: This describes technical improvements made to enable 3D correction.

claim: The modifications to enable 3D correction reduce the time required to perform motion correction by a factor of 30 for typical volumetric datasets.
source: These modifications reduce the time required to perform motion correction by a factor of 30 for typical volumetric datasets and open the door to online motion correction in the future.
evidence: This claim is supported by timing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The modifications to enable 3D correction open the door to online motion correction in the future.
source: These modifications reduce the time required to perform motion correction by a factor of 30 for typical volumetric datasets and open the door to online motion correction in the future.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future applications based on the performance improvements.

claim: Motions covering a broad range of physiologically relevant motions, from respiration to the heartbeat, can be effectively compensated when the magnitude of the motion is ~10% of the FOV.
source: We found that motions covering a broad range of physiologically relevant motions, from respiration to the heartbeat can be effectively compensated when the magnitude of the motion was ~10% of the FOV,
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Significantly large motions, up to 30% of the FOV, can be corrected at lower frequencies.
source: while significantly large motions, up to 30% of the FOV could be corrected at lower frequencies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Faster motions may be compensated by using faster scan rate, for example by employing a resonant scanner.
source: We note that faster motions still may be compensated by using faster scan rate, for example by employing a resonant scanner.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the observed relationship between scan rate and correction quality.

claim: The difference in quality of correction of motions in the fast and slow axis is due to the frequency with which different positions are sampled during the acquisition.
source: The difference in quality of correction of motions in the fast and slow axis is due to the frequency with which different positions are sampled during the acquisition.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the physics of laser scanning microscopy.

claim: Acquiring a 256 × 256 image at 1000 Hz means that every x-position will be sampled every millisecond while every y-position is sampled every 256 milliseconds.
source: Acquiring a 256 × 256 image at 1000 Hz means that every x-position will be sampled every millisecond (albeit at a different y position), while every y-position is sampled every 256 milliseconds.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the scan pattern and timing.

claim: A motion purely in the fast scan (x-) direction will appear as a wave-like motion while a motion in the slow axis will appear to compress and stretch the image.
source: A motion purely in the fast scan (x-) direction will appear as a wave-like motion while a motion in the slow axis will appear to compress and stretch the image and, for sufficiently large motion, whole lines may be missed.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the scan pattern and motion direction.

claim: The data constrain the estimate of motion in the fast axis more strongly than in the slow axis.
source: This means that the data constrain the estimate of motion in the fast axis more strongly than in the slow axis.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the sampling frequency differences.

claim: Galene can compensate for a range of physiological motions and retrieve both cellular and subcellular resolution.
source: We confirmed these results using intravital FLIM-FRET biosensor imaging data and multispectral intensity-based data to demonstrate that we can compensate for a range of physiological motions. We showed that we can correct for motion occurring both between frames and within frames which otherwise render the image unintelligible and thereby retrieve both cellular and subcellular resolution.
evidence: This is a summary of the results demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

claim: Galene will enable researchers to apply functional imaging modalities in contexts previously inaccessible due to excessive motion.
source: This will enable researchers to apply functional imaging modalities in contexts previously inaccessible due to excessive motion and therefore extend acquisition times, providing higher signal to noise (or using a lower excitation power to prevent tissue damage or photo-bleaching).
evidence: This is inferred from the demonstrated capabilities of Galene.

claim: Other recent applications of intravital FRET investigating RhoA, Erk signalling, cancer stemness, PKA in vascular permeability and stromal targeting in melanoma could benefit from the Galene approach.
source: Other recent applications of intravital FRET investigating, for example, RhoA (Nobis et al., 2017), intricate Erk signalling propagation events from in the skin (Hiratsuka et al., 2015) or cancer stemness (Kumagai et al., 2015), PKA in vascular permeability (Yamauchi et al., 2016) and stromal targeting in melanoma (Hirata et al., 2015) could benefit from this approach.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications based on the demonstrated capabilities, with citations to relevant work.

claim: Scopolamine induces a significant activation of Rac1 in intestinal tissue, which would compromise any study of Rac1 signalling in this context.
source: We observed that, although scopolamine effectively inhibited sample motion, it induces a significant activation of Rac1. This would compromise any study of Rac1 signalling in this context, illustrating the potential pitfalls of pharmacological approaches to inhibiting sample motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The extensive physiological motion observed in the liver not only significantly degrades the image but also introduces a significant artefact into the FLIM readout of the Src-FRET activity by mixing the FRET signal with the autofluorescence background.
source: The extensive physiological motion observed in the liver not only significantly degrades the image but also, by mixing the FRET signal with the autofluorescence background, introduces a significant artefact into the FLIM readout of the Src-FRET activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the comparison of corrected and uncorrected data in Figure 5.

claim: Using Galene, a significant delay in Src activity was observed after priming with Fasudil at early time points, providing a potential mechanism for the significant reduction in metastatic colonisation.
source: Using Galene, we observe a significant delay in Src activity after priming with Fasudil at early time points, providing a potential mechanism for the significant reduction in metastatic colonisation observed in endpoint metastatic burden experiments (Vennin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results shown in Figure 5, with citation to prior work.

claim: The approach demonstrated may have wider applications in other metastatic cancers where early adhesion events are difficult to study.
source: As highlighted above, this may have wider applications in other metastatic cancers where early adhesion events are difficult to study.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: This approach could be readily applied to confocal endoscopic systems to allow TCSPC FLIM acquisitions in an intraoperative context.
source: This approach could be readily applied to confocal endoscopic systems (Kennedy et al., 2010; Siegel et al., 2003; Sparks et al., in press; Sun et al., 2013) to allow TCSPC FLIM acquisitions in an intraoperative context, for example for tumour margin assessment (Gorpas et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications with citations to relevant work.

claim: The processing time for motion correction is typically significantly shorter than data acquisition, even for high speed 3D applications.
source: For such applications, this approach could readily be extended to enable real time correction of FLIM data, as the processing time is typically significantly shorter than data acquisition, even for high speed 3D applications.
evidence: This is based on the performance measurements described in the manuscript.

claim: The system could be combined with a hardware-based lateral motion correction approach that can track large displacements to enable high fidelity correction when the microscope itself is moving.
source: In principle, this system could be combined with a hardware-based lateral motion correction approach (Sherlock et al., 2018), that can track large displacements to enable high fidelity correction when the microscope itself is moving.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future developments with citation to relevant work.

claim: Combining hardware and software motion correction would allow a macro scale FLIM map to be constructed by freely moving the imaging system across the sample.
source: This would allow, for example, a macro scale FLIM map to be constructed by freely moving the imaging system across the sample.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of combined hardware and software correction.

claim: Galene will allow researchers to apply time resolved functional imaging in a broader range of contexts, relaxing previous restrictions on sample stability and imaging duration.
source: Galene will therefore allow researchers to apply time resolved functional imaging in a broader range of contexts, relaxing previous restrictions on sample stability and imaging duration and make use of data which would have previously been discarded, in vitro, in vivo and in the clinic.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the impact of Galene based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claim: Galene can make use of data which would have previously been discarded.
source: Galene will therefore allow researchers to apply time resolved functional imaging in a broader range of contexts, relaxing previous restrictions on sample stability and imaging duration and make use of data which would have previously been discarded, in vitro, in vivo and in the clinic.
evidence: This is inferred from the capability to correct motion in post-processing.

claim: The source code for Galene is freely available alongside compiled executables for Windows and Mac at http://galene.flimfit.org/.
source: The source code for Galene is freely available alongside compiled executable for Windows and Mac at http://galene.flimfit.org/.
evidence: This is a statement about the availability of the software.
